passage: In Rashmi's small town, the only quiet place in the evenings was the back room of her uncle's cloth shop, and that is where she made her sheets. One chapter, one page, no more. For History that meant choosing: three dates out of fifteen, one map, the two causes every past paper asked about. "You're leaving things out," said her cousin Rafiq, reading over her shoulder. "That's the point," Rashmi said. "If I can't fit it on one page, I don't really know what matters." The Geography sheets were mostly diagrams: monsoon arrows, soil types in coloured blocks. By the last week she had forty-two pages clipped into a folder. While others flipped through fat guides, Rashmi read her whole syllabus twice a day, sitting on a bolt of cotton cloth.

qa.q: How many pages did Rashmi have by the last week?
qa.a: Forty-two pages, clipped into a folder.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel about leaving things out?
qa.a: She felt confident and clear about it, seeing the choosing as the whole point.

qa.q: What else could Rashmi do with the sheets in the last week?
qa.a: Cover each sheet and try to rewrite it from memory, so reading turns into active recall.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see the one-page rule?
qa.a: Rafiq is doubtful at first about the missing details, but may see its value when Rashmi can read the whole syllabus twice a day.

grounding: Shows a student condensing each chapter onto one page, being forced to choose essentials, and reading the sheets in the final week.

passage: Three weeks before his final exams in Copenhagen, Emil laid a stack of blank sheets on his desk and made a rule: one chapter, one page. Chemistry went first. He had to decide which of the nine reactions in chapter one actually mattered, which formulas he would forget and which he never would, which diagram told the whole story. It took an hour a chapter, longer than rereading. His friend Rafael, sprawled on the bed, asked why he didn't just read the textbook again. "Because the book lets me think everything matters," Emil said. "The page doesn't." In the final week he carried the sheets everywhere: on the tram, in the queue at the bakery. Thirty-one pages for three subjects. The night before Chemistry, he read all of that subject's pages and went to bed early.

qa.q: How many pages did Emil make for three subjects?
How might Emil feel the night before Chemistry?
qa.a: He probably feels calm and prepared, able to read the whole subject and still go to bed early.

qa.q: What makes the one-page rule useful, according to Emil?
qa.a: It forces him to decide what really matters, while the textbook lets everything seem important.

qa.q: How might Rafael see the hour spent on each page?
qa.a: Rafael thinks rereading would be quicker, and may be surprised that the slower method gives Emil a compact set of notes for the final week.

grounding: Shows a student making one-page summaries per chapter, choosing essentials, and reading them in the final week.
